From scattered churn signals to a shared retention workflow

Overview

Competitor and churn signals from client calls were scattered across Google Chat and personal spreadsheets, leaving gaps in the information available for retention planning.

I designed a connected workflow: AI flags mentions, n8n prepares a HubSpot questionnaire, and account managers have three days to review it before submission. A daily dashboard sync gives stakeholders a shared view while distinguishing reviewed records from automatic submissions.

Key Impact

83% reported increase in response rate

An increase in the existing churn-risk response rate, reported from the project. Automated collection and daily shared reporting gave retention stakeholders a centralized basis for action.

The problemWorkflowManager reviewDashboardExplore the demoReflection

Important signals depended on someone passing them along.

Client conversations were recorded in Gong, but competitor mentions and churn risks still depended on account managers relaying them through Google Chat or personal spreadsheets. Information was fragmented, and some signals never reached the people responsible for responding.

Stakeholders needed a common place to understand emerging risks and prepare a retention plan.

Connect collection, review, and visibility.

  1. Prepare the record

    Flag mentions in Gong and prefill a HubSpot questionnaire through n8n, giving the account manager a signal to review.

  2. Define a review window

    Allow three days for review, then submit unactioned questionnaires automatically. Coverage improves only if unreviewed information stays identifiable.

  3. Share a common view

    Sync daily to a company-wide dashboard, so retention stakeholders can plan from the same collected information.

Before

Reporting depended on manual follow-through

  1. Gong recordingsClient conversations contain competitor and churn mentions.
  2. Manual reportingAccount managers relay signals through Google Chat or personal spreadsheets.
  3. Fragmented informationScattered records leave stakeholders with an incomplete picture.
After

A connected path from signal to shared visibility

  1. DetectAI trackers flag competitor and churn mentions.
  2. Preparen8n sends the relevant account manager a prefilled HubSpot questionnaire.
  3. ReviewThe account manager has three days to review the information.
  4. SubmitManager-reviewed information proceeds; unactioned questionnaires submit automatically.
  5. ShareData syncs daily to a centralized company-wide dashboard.

Automatic submission applies only when the three-day window passes without action. It does not establish human validation.

Workflow explainer reconstructed from the confirmed project sequence.

Review the signal, then add the relationship context.

In the revised prototype, a review queue brings the account, assigned manager, deadline, time remaining, and status together. Opening a record separates AI-detected intelligence from the manager’s validation.

The prefilled form includes the conversation excerpt and AI-generated summary. The manager can assess accuracy and switching intent, clarify the offer, add context, and recommend a next action. A visible countdown and three-day policy explain what happens if no action is taken.

Approved

A manager has reviewed and approved the record in the prototype.

Auto-Submitted

The review window expired. Original AI-detected details enter reporting without manager confirmation.

See the pattern. Keep the context.

The revised overview brings trends, risk distribution, competitor comparisons, priority accounts, and recent activity into one view. The intelligence table then connects each mention to its client context, account manager, detection date, and review status.

Search and filters support different questions: which competitor is appearing, which accounts need attention, and which signals have been reviewed. An account detail drawer keeps the excerpt and review history available for closer inspection.

Coverage and confidence need to travel together.

The original project made churn-risk information accessible to more stakeholders and supported faster preparation of retention action plans. These are reported project outcomes; the prototype’s account counts, revenue figures, and risk scores are not impact measures.

The revised prototype makes the difference between approval and automatic submission visible. That distinction matters: collecting more information is useful only when people can judge its reliability. I would next test whether stakeholders can identify unreviewed signals and decide when follow-up is needed.
